standards_base: South Carolina College- and Career-Ready Science Standards 2021
notes: Performance Targets describe observable features of student performance for each Performance Expectation (PE). They are not a curriculum. Each PE names one dedicated SEP and CCC, but full three-dimensional instruction draws on the whole range of SEPs/CCCs. See EOCEP Biology 1 State Assessment Specifications for item-writing/assessment-mode rules distinct from classroom use.

domains.domain_name: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

standards.performance_expectation: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins, which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include identification of specific cell or tissue types, whole body systems, specific protein structures and functions, or the biochemistry of protein synthesis.

sep.name: Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions
sep.description: Construct an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources (including models, peer review, simulations, theories, students' own investigations) and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future.

dci.name: Structure and Function
dci.text: Systems of specialized cells within organisms help them perform the essential functions of life. All cells contain genetic information, in the form of DNA. Genes are specific regions within the extremely large DNA molecules that form the chromosomes. Genes contain the instructions that code for the formation of molecules called proteins, which carry out most of the work of cells to perform the essential functions of life. Proteins provide structural components, serve as signaling devices, regulate cell activities, and determine the performance of cells through their enzymatic actions.

dci.name: Inheritance of Traits
dci.text: The sequence of nucleotides spells out the information in a gene. DNA controls the expression of proteins by being transcribed into a "messenger" RNA, which is translated in turn by the cellular machinery into a protein.

ccc.name: Structure and Function
ccc.description: Investigating or designing new systems or structures requires a detailed examination of the properties of different materials, the structures of different components, and connections of components to reveal its function.

proteins carry out the essential functions of life

DNA contains regions called genes

proper functioning of many proteins is necessary for the proper functioning of cells

standards.performance_expectation: Use a model to illustrate the role of cellular division (mitosis) and differentiation in producing and maintaining complex organisms.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on normal cell division as well as instances in which cell division is uncontrolled (e.g., cancer).
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include specific gene control mechanisms or rote memorization of the steps of mitosis.

sep.name: Developing and Using Models
sep.description: Use a model based on evidence to illustrate and/or predict the relationships between systems or between components of a system.

dci.name: Growth and Development of Organisms
dci.text: In multicellular organisms, individual cells grow and then divide via a process called mitosis, thereby allowing the organism to grow (and repair). The organism begins as a single cell (fertilized egg) that divides successively to produce many cells, with each parent cell passing identical genetic material (two variants of each chromosome pair) to both daughter cells. Cellular division and differentiation produce and maintain a complex organism, composed of systems of tissues and organs that work together to meet the needs of the whole organism.

ccc.name: Systems and System Models
ccc.description: Models (e.g., physical, mathematical, computer models) can be used to simulate systems and interactions—including energy, matter, and information flows—within and between systems at different scales.

a multicellular organism as a collection of differentiated cells
phases of the cell cycle (G1, S, G2, M, cytokinesis, checkpoints)
relationships: daughter cells receive identical genetic information from a parent cell

when cells bypass checkpoints, uncontrolled cell division (limited to cancer) may occur
differences between cell types within a multicellular organism are due to gene expression, not genetic differences

standards.performance_expectation: Use a model to illustrate how photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on explaining inputs and outputs of matter and the transfer and transformation of energy in photosynthesis by plants and other photosynthesizing organisms. Examples of models could include diagrams, chemical equations, and conceptual models.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include specific biochemical steps.

sep.name: Developing and Using Models
sep.description: Use a model based on evidence to illustrate the relationships between systems or between components of a system.

dci.name: Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms
dci.text: The process of photosynthesis converts light energy to stored chemical energy by converting carbon dioxide plus water into sugars plus released oxygen.

ccc.name: Energy and Matter
ccc.description: Changes of energy and matter in a system can be described in terms of energy and matter flows into, out of, and within that system.

model_components: chemical energy transfer between light-dependent and light-independent reactions (ATP/ADP, NADPH/NADP+)
connections: transfer of matter and flow of energy between an organism and its environment during photosynthesis
transfer of matter and flow of energy within the cell of a photosynthetic organism
photosynthesis results in storage of energy in the difference between the energies of chemical bonds of inputs and outputs

standards.performance_expectation: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements to form amino acids and other large carbon-based molecules necessary for essential life processes.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on using evidence from models and simulations to support explanations of how the products of photosynthesis can be used to form the molecules of life.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include the details of the specific chemical reactions or molecular identification of macromolecules.

sep.name: Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions
sep.description: Construct and revise an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future.

dci.name: Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms
dci.text: The sugar molecules formed contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen: the hydrocarbon backbones are used to make amino acids and other carbon-based molecules that can be assembled into larger molecules (such as proteins or DNA), used for essential life functions. As matter and energy flow through organizational levels of living systems, chemical elements are recombined to form different products.

ccc.name: Energy and Matter
ccc.description: Changes of energy and matter in a system can be described in terms of energy and matter flows into, out of, and within that system.

standards.performance_expectation: Use a model to illustrate that cellular respiration is a chemical process whereby the bonds of food molecules are broken and the bonds in new compounds are formed, resulting in a net transfer of energy.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on the conceptual understanding of the inputs and outputs of the processes of aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment should not include identification of the steps or specific processes involved in cellular respiration nor specific types of fermentation. Assessment should be limited to comparing efficiency of aerobic and anaerobic cellular respiration.

sep.name: Developing and Using Models
sep.description: Use a model based on evidence to illustrate the relationships between systems or between components of a system.

dci.name: Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms
dci.text: As matter and energy flow through different organizational levels of living systems, chemical elements are recombined in different ways to form different products. Cellular respiration is a chemical process in which the bonds of food molecules and oxygen molecules are broken, and new compounds are formed that can transport energy to muscles. Anaerobic cellular respiration follows a different and less efficient chemical pathway to provide energy in cells.

ccc.name: Energy and Matter
ccc.description: Energy cannot be created or destroyed—it only moves between one place and another place, between objects and/or fields, or between systems.

model_components: glycolysis, Kreb's cycle, Electron Transport Chain, fermentation
relationships: energy transfer and conservation of matter between subsystems
connections: cellular respiration releases energy as matter is rearranged and bonds are broken/formed, but matter and energy are neither created nor destroyed
when oxygen is not available, cells use fermentation to maintain ATP production, with a marked decrease in efficiency vs. aerobic respiration

standards.performance_expectation: Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of biotic and abiotic factors that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on quantitative analysis and comparison of the relationships among interdependent factors including boundaries, resources, climate, and challenges. Examples of mathematical comparisons could include graphs, charts, histograms, or population changes gathered from simulations and historical data sets. Examples of scales could be a pond versus an ocean.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include deriving mathematical equations to make comparisons.

sep.name: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking
sep.description: Use mathematical and/or computational representations of phenomena or design solutions to support explanations.

dci.name: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems
dci.text: Ecosystems have carrying capacities, which are limits to the numbers of organisms and populations they can support. These limits result from factors such as the availability of living and nonliving resources and challenges such as predation, competition, and disease. This fundamental tension affects the abundance (number of individuals) of species in any given ecosystem.

ccc.name: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity
ccc.description: The significance of a phenomenon is dependent on the scale, proportion, and quantity at which it occurs.

representation: mathematical/computational models (trends, averages, histograms, graphs, spreadsheets) of population changes from historical data/simulations
data on numbers/types of organisms, boundaries, resources, climate
analysis: identify interdependence of abiotic/biotic factors and effect on carrying capacity
predict resulting effect on carrying capacity of a change in factors
identify factors with the largest effect on carrying capacity for an identified population

standards.performance_expectation: Develop a model to illustrate the role of photosynthesis and cellular respiration in the cycling of carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include the specific chemical steps of photosynthesis and respiration.

sep.name: Developing and Using Models
sep.description: Develop a model based on evidence to illustrate the relationships between systems or components of a system.

dci.name: Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems
dci.text: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are important components of the carbon cycle, in which carbon is exchanged among the biosphere, atmosphere, oceans, and geosphere through chemical, physical, geological, and biological processes.

dci.name: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life
dci.text: The main way that solar energy is captured and stored on Earth is through the complex chemical process known as photosynthesis. (secondary)

ccc.name: Systems and System Models
ccc.description: Models can be used to simulate systems and interactions—including energy, matter, and information flows—within and between systems at different scales.

cellular respiration rearranges matter to release stored chemical energy used for essential life processes

standards.performance_expectation: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution for reducing the impacts of human activities on biodiversity and ecosystem health.

sep.name: Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions
sep.description: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution to a complex real-world problem, based on scientific knowledge, student-generated sources of evidence, prioritized criteria, and trade off considerations.

dci.name: Ecosystem Dynamics, Functioning, and Resilience
dci.text: Anthropogenic changes (induced by human activity) in the environment—including habitat destruction, pollution, introduction of invasive species, overexploitation, and climate change—can disrupt an ecosystem and threaten the survival of some species.

dci.name: Biodiversity and Humans
dci.text: Human activity is having adverse impacts on biodiversity through overpopulation, overexploitation, habitat destruction, pollution, introduction of invasive species, and climate change, with potential for biological extinctions and decreased biodiversity. (secondary)

dci.name: Developing Possible Solutions
dci.text: When evaluating solutions, it is important to take into account a range of constraints including cost, safety, reliability and aesthetics and to consider social, cultural and environmental impacts. (secondary)

ccc.name: Stability and Change
ccc.description: Much of science deals with constructing explanations of how things change and how they remain stable.

design: design a solution addressing overpopulation, overexploitation, habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species, and/or climate change

domains.domain_name: Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits

standards.performance_expectation: Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from (1) new genetic combinations through meiosis, (2) viable errors occurring during replication, and/or (3) mutations caused by environmental factors.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on using data to support arguments for the way genetic variation occurs.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include the phases of meiosis or the biochemical mechanism of specific steps in the process.

sep.name: Engaging in Argument from Evidence
sep.description: Make and defend a claim based on evidence about the natural world that reflects scientific knowledge and student-generated evidence.

dci.name: Variation of Traits
dci.text: In sexual reproduction, chromosomes can sometimes swap sections during meiosis, creating new genetic combinations and more genetic variation. DNA replication errors result in mutations, which are also a source of genetic variation. Environmental factors can also cause mutations in genes, and viable mutations are inherited. Environmental factors also affect expression of traits, and hence affect the probability of occurrences of traits in a population.

ccc.name: Cause and Effect
ccc.description: Empirical evidence is required to differentiate between cause and correlation and make claims about specific causes and effects.

evidence: variation in genetic material naturally results during meiosis from crossing over and independent assortment
genetic mutations can occur due to replication errors and environmental factors (mutagen)
genetic material is inheritable
reasoning: genetic mutations produce genetic variation between cells or organisms
genetic variations produced by mutation and meiosis can be inherited

standards.performance_expectation: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a population.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on the use of mathematics to describe the probability of traits as it relates to genetic and environmental factors in the expression of traits.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include Hardy-Weinberg or Chi-square analysis.

sep.name: Analyzing and Interpreting Data
sep.description: Apply concepts of statistics and probability (including determining function fits to data, slope, intercept, and correlation coefficient for linear fits) to scientific and engineering questions and problems, using digital tools when feasible.

dci.name: Variation of Traits
dci.text: Environmental factors also affect expression of traits, and hence affect the probability of occurrences of traits in a population. Thus, the variation and distribution of traits observed depends on both genetic and environmental factors.

ccc.name: Scale, Proportion, and Quantity
ccc.description: Algebraic thinking is used to examine scientific data and predict the effect of a change in one variable on another (e.g., linear growth vs. exponential growth).

identifying_relationships: analyze data (probability measures) to determine relationship between a trait's occurrence and environmental factors

standards.performance_expectation: Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines of empirical evidence.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on students' conceptual understanding of the role each line of evidence has relating to common ancestry and biological evolution. Examples of evidence could include similarities in DNA sequences, anatomical structures, and order of appearance of structures in embryological development.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment is limited to conceptual explanations of the evidence for biological evolution and is not extended to the lines of evidence for specific species. Assessment does not include classification of organisms.

sep.name: Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information
sep.description: Communicate scientific information (e.g., about phenomena and/or the process of development and the design and performance of a proposed process or system) in multiple formats (including orally, graphically, textually, and mathematically).

dci.name: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity
dci.text: Genetic information, like the fossil record, provides evidence of evolution. DNA sequences vary among species, but there are many overlaps; the ongoing branching that produces multiple lines of descent can be inferred by comparing DNA sequences of different organisms. Such information is also derivable from similarities/differences in amino acid sequences and from anatomical and embryological evidence.

dci.name: Influence of Engineering, Technology, and Science on Society and the Natural World
dci.text: The understanding of evolutionary relationships has recently been greatly accelerated by using new molecular tools to study biology.

ccc.name: Patterns
ccc.description: Different patterns may be observed at each of the scales at which a system is studied and can provide evidence for causality in explanations of phenomena.

communication: use and cite at least two formats (oral, graphical, textual, mathematical) to communicate evidence
connections: DNA sequences vary among species but have many similarities
similarities of amino acid sequences even when DNA sequences differ; the triplet codon pattern is universal
patterns of anatomical and embryological similarities

standards.performance_expectation: Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the heritable genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for limited resources, and (4) the proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in the environment.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on using evidence to explain the influence each of the four factors has on the number of organisms, behaviors, morphology, or physiology in terms of ability to compete for limited resources and subsequent survival of individuals and adaptation of species. Examples of evidence could include mathematical models such as simple distribution graphs and proportional reasoning.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include other mechanisms of evolution, such as genetic drift, gene flow through migration, and co-evolution.

sep.name: Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions
sep.description: Construct an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future.

dci.name: Natural Selection
dci.text: Natural selection occurs only if there is both (1) variation in the genetic information between organisms in a population and (2) variation in the expression of that genetic information (trait variation) that leads to differences in performance among individuals.

dci.name: Adaptation
dci.text: Evolution is driven by the interaction of four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for an environment's limited supply of resources, and (4) the ensuing proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in that environment.

ccc.name: Cause and Effect
ccc.description: Empirical evidence is required to differentiate between cause and correlation and make claims about specific causes and effects.

standards.performance_expectation: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on using data to provide evidence for how specific biotic and abiotic differences in ecosystems (such as ranges of seasonal temperature, long-term climate change, acidity, light, geographic barriers, or evolution of other organisms) contribute to a change in gene frequency over time, leading to adaptation of populations.
standards.state_assessment_boundary: Assessment does not include allele frequency calculations.

sep.name: Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions
sep.description: Construct an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future.

dci.name: Adaptation
dci.text: Natural selection leads to adaptation, that is, to a population dominated by organisms that are anatomically, behaviorally, and physiologically well suited to survive and reproduce in a specific environment. The differential survival and reproduction of organisms with an advantageous heritable trait leads to an increase in the proportion of individuals with the trait and a decrease in the proportion without it.

standards.performance_expectation: Evaluate the evidence supporting claims that changes in environmental conditions may result in (1) increases in the number of individuals of some species, (2) the emergence of new species over time, and (3) the extinction of other species.
standards.clarification_statement: Emphasis is on determining cause and effect relationships for how changes to the environment such as deforestation, fishing, application of fertilizers, drought, flood, and the rate of change of the environment affect distribution or disappearance of traits in species.

sep.name: Engaging in Argument from Evidence

dci.name: Adaptation
dci.text: Changes in the physical environment, whether naturally occurring or human induced, have contributed to the expansion of some species, the emergence of new distinct species as populations diverge under different conditions, and the decline—and sometimes extinction—of some species. Species become extinct because they can no longer survive and reproduce in their altered environment.
